etymology: Old English gēan- (against) + secgan (to say): literally to say-against. Renders the Greek antilegō, “to speak against, contradict, oppose in words.”
biblical_def: To gainsay is to speak against—to contradict, oppose, deny, refute. The Old English construction is precise (gain-, against; -say, speak), and the KJV uses the verb to render the Greek antilegō in contexts where the contradiction is verbal and public. Christ promises His witnesses such a gift of utterance that all your adversaries shall not be able to gainsay nor resist (Luke 21:15)—the apostolic word will be such that opponents cannot effectively contradict it. Titus 1:9 sets the verb at the qualifications for elders: the bishop must be holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers—the gainsayers being those who actively speak against sound apostolic doctrine. Romans 10:21 uses the verb of Israel’s long history of resisting God’s pleading: all day long I have stretched forth my hands unto a disobedient and gainsaying people. Jude 11 names the gainsaying of Core—Korah’s contradiction of Moses’ appointed leadership and presumption against the Aaronic priesthood, ending in his and his company being swallowed alive by the earth (Num 16). The verb’s biblical pattern therefore traces three uses: the gainsaying of unbelievers against the gospel (which Christ promises His witnesses shall not prevail); the gainsaying of false teachers against sound doctrine (which the elder must refute by sound doctrine); and the gainsaying of the rebellious against God’s appointed leadership (which incurs severe judgment). To gainsay is therefore not merely to disagree but to set one’s speech actively against what God has spoken, established, or commissioned—a serious verb for a serious posture, and one that the KJV retains in its full Anglo-Saxon weight where modern translations often soften it.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines GAINSAY as to contradict; to oppose in words; to deny or declare not to be true what another has said.
webster_full: GAINSAY, v.t. — To contradict; to oppose in words; to deny or declare not to be true what another has said; to controvert. Adversaries shall not be able to gainsay nor resist (Luke 21:15).
GAINSAYER, n. — One who contradicts or denies what is alleged; an opposer. That he may be able...to convince the gainsayers (Tit 1:9).
scriptures: Luke 21:15
For I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries shall not be able to gainsay nor resist.
Titus 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
Romans 10:21
But to Israel he saith, All day long I have stretched forth my hands unto a disobedient and gainsaying people.
Jude 1:11
Woe unto them! for they have gone in the way of Cain, and ran greedily after the error of Balaam for reward, and perished in the gainsaying of Core.
corruption_summary: Gainsay is corrupted by the modernizing impulse that has replaced the precise KJV vocabulary with the colorless contradict or oppose—losing the Anglo-Saxon weight of say-against—and by the contemporary collapse of the very category of speaking-against-God’s-Word that the verb names, in a culture where every assertion is treated as one valid opinion among many.
corruption_paragraphs: Modernizing translations have widely replaced gainsay with the colorless contradict, oppose, or argue against. The replacement is grammatically defensible; the loss is rhetorical and pastoral. Gainsay carries the Anglo-Saxon directness of say-against: it names a speech-act of active verbal opposition, with weight, with risk, with seriousness. Contradict in modern usage has been domesticated into the polite register of academic disagreement; gainsay still carries the older weight of Korah’s rebellion and the gospel-opponent’s public defiance. The KJV’s retention of the word is therefore not archaism for its own sake but the preservation of a vocabulary register that the modern equivalents have lost. Readers who learn to hear the KJV in its own idiom recover access to a register of speech-seriousness that the modern translations, for all their accessibility, have inadvertently flattened.

The deeper contemporary corruption is the collapse of the very category the verb names. Gainsay requires a fixed standard against which the contradiction is measured—God’s Word, sound doctrine, the appointed leadership. In a culture where every assertion is treated as one valid opinion among many, no claim has the standing to be gainsaid: there is only the endless equivalence of competing views. Scripture refuses this. There is a faithful word which is to be held fast; there is sound doctrine by which gainsayers are to be convinced; there is God’s pleading at which Israel’s gainsaying was judged; there are appointed offices and ordinances which Korah’s gainsaying could not overturn. Recover both ends: the precise vocabulary that names the speech-act, and the substantive standards (Word, doctrine, leadership) without which the speech-act has no biblical referent. The elder who can convince the gainsayers by sound doctrine is the elder Titus 1:9 requires, and the church saturated with such elders is the church that holds its faithful word across the centuries against every contradiction.
roots_summary: Old English gēan- (against) + secgan (to say) — literally say-against; renders Greek antilegō, the verbal opposition that contradicts God’s Word, sound doctrine, or appointed leadership.
roots_lines: Greek antilegō (G483) — to speak against, contradict, oppose in words (Luke 2:34; 21:15; John 19:12; Acts 13:45; 28:19, 22; Rom 10:21; Tit 1:9; 2:9).
Greek antilogia (G485) — the act of speaking against, contradiction, dispute (Heb 6:16; 7:7; 12:3; Jude 11, “the gainsaying of Core”).
Old English gēan- — against (the prefix giving the verb its directional sense).
Old English secgan — to say (the root of modern say).
usage: I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries shall not be able to gainsay nor resist—Christ’s promise to His witnesses that gainsayers cannot prevail.
Three biblical uses of gainsay: unbelievers against the gospel, false teachers against sound doctrine, the rebellious against appointed leadership.
Modern translations replace gainsay with the colorless contradict; the KJV retains the Anglo-Saxon weight of say-against, a register the modern equivalents have lost.

etymology: Archaic past participle of help; Old English holpen (helped, aided), past participle of helpan. Renders the Greek antilambanō, “to take hold of, help, support,” in Luke 1:54.
biblical_def: Holpen is the archaic past participle of help—an Old English form that the KJV preserves in one of its most celebrated passages, the Magnificat: he hath holpen his servant Israel, in remembrance of his mercy (Luke 1:54). Modern English long ago shifted the past participle to helped; the KJV retains the older form, which carries a distinctive cadence and an antique dignity. The Greek behind it—antilambanō—means literally to take hold of in turn, to take hold against, and pictures God reaching out to take hold of His servant Israel against the weight of her need and her enemies. The verb’s biblical pattern, broader than this single archaic-English form, traces God’s sustained help of His people across redemptive history. He holpen His servant Israel in remembrance of His mercy, the Magnificat says; He holpen them out of Egypt by the hand of Moses; He holpen them through the wilderness with manna and water; He holpen them in the conquest by the sword of the angel of the LORD; He holpen them in the days of the judges by the deliverers He raised up; He holpen them by the hand of David against the Philistines and the surrounding kingdoms; He holpen them through the captivity by the providences that preserved a remnant; and supremely He has holpen them in the sending of the Saviour, the Son of Mary, the seed of Abraham, the Son of David, the One whose advent the Magnificat itself celebrates. Holpen as a word therefore carries a long memory: the long history of God’s help to His people, against which the present help (Christ’s incarnation) is the consummate instance. The KJV’s retention of the antique form is fitting; the antique form carries the antique memory.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines HOLPEN as the past participle of help (archaic), as in the Magnificat: he hath holpen his servant Israel (Luke 1:54).
webster_full: HOLPEN, ppr. or pp. — Archaic past participle of help; helped. He hath holpen his servant Israel, in remembrance of his mercy (Luke 1:54). The modern past participle is helped, but the archaic form is preserved in the KJV.
HELP, v.t. — To aid; to assist; to lend strength or means towards effecting a purpose; as, to help a man in his work.
scriptures: He hath holpen his servant Israel, in remembrance of his mercy; As he spake to our fathers, to Abraham, and to his seed for ever.
Acts 26:22
Having therefore obtained help of God, I continue unto this day, witnessing both to small and great...
Hebrews 4:16
Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need.
Psalm 121:1-2
I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help. My help cometh from the LORD, which made heaven and earth.
corruption_summary: Holpen is corrupted (by the standards of modern accessibility) by retaining the archaic form most readers no longer recognize—but the loss of the form, in modern translations, is also the loss of the cadence and dignity by which the Magnificat’s long memory of God’s help across the generations is rhetorically carried.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern translations uniformly replace holpen with the contemporary helped, on grounds of accessibility. The trade is real. Helped is immediately understood; holpen requires explanation. But what is lost in the modernization is not merely a vocabulary item but a register: the antique form carries the antique memory, the Magnificat’s long backward look across the centuries of God’s help to Israel is borne by the language that itself comes from centuries past. He hath holpen his servant Israel, in remembrance of his mercy, as he spake to our fathers, to Abraham, and to his seed for ever—the cadence of the verse is doing work that the flatter modern he has helped his servant Israel, remembering to be merciful cannot replicate. The KJV reader who learns the antique form recovers access to the cadence and dignity by which Mary’s song reaches back across the generations of Israel’s covenant history.

This is the general pastoral case for the KJV’s antique vocabulary, of which holpen is one specimen. The archaic forms are not preserved as obstacles to comprehension but as bearers of a rhetorical register modern English has largely lost. The reader who acquires the small skill of reading them recovers access not only to the meanings but to the depth of address Scripture in its English tradition has been given. The case is not against modern translations as such (which have their proper uses) but against the assumption that modernization is sheer gain. Holpen is a small case that illustrates the larger pattern: the KJV is not merely accurate; it is rhetorically formed in a register that has shaped English Christian piety for four centuries, and the saint who reads it in its own idiom hears Scripture in a register the modernization has, sometimes, quietly lost.
roots_summary: Old English holpen, past participle of helpan (to help); renders Greek antilambanō (to take hold of, help, support—Luke 1:54); preserved in the KJV in the Magnificat’s celebrated retrospection of God’s help to His servant Israel across the generations.
roots_lines: Old English holpen — archaic past participle of helpan, to help.
Greek antilambanō (G482) — to take hold of, help, support (Luke 1:54; Acts 20:35; 1 Tim 6:2).
Hebrew ‘āzar (H5826) — to help, aid (the great OT help-verb).
Hebrew ‘ezer (H5828) — help, aid (Gen 2:18, the woman as a help meet for man).
usage: He hath holpen his servant Israel, in remembrance of his mercy—the Magnificat’s long backward look across the centuries of God’s help.
Holpen retains the antique cadence by which Mary’s song reaches across the generations; the modern helped flattens the register.
The case for the KJV’s antique vocabulary is not against modernization as such but for the recognition that the older forms carry a rhetorical register the modern equivalents have, sometimes, lost.

etymology: Latin lucrum, “gain, profit.” The KJV uses lucre almost exclusively in the disapproving phrase filthy lucre (aischrokerdēs in Greek), naming dishonest or unworthy gain.
biblical_def: Lucre in the KJV is almost always disapproving and almost always paired with filthy—filthy lucre—to render the Greek aischrokerdēs (literally shamefully-greedy) and its cousins. The phrase is most famously the qualification for church officers. Elders are to be not greedy of filthy lucre (1 Tim 3:3; 1 Tim 3:8 of deacons; Tit 1:7 of bishops); 1 Pet 5:2 charges elders to feed the flock not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind. The qualification is severe and structural. The minister’s motive in his service must not be money—not the salary, not the speaker’s honoraria, not the book royalties, not the platform’s profitability, not any form of pecuniary gain. Where the motive of money has entered the ministry, the office has been corrupted at its root, and the Spirit’s warning is sharp. Paul applies the same disapproval to false teachers generally: teaching things which they ought not, for filthy lucre’s sake (Tit 1:11)—the willingness to teach error for money is the marker of those who must be stopped. Beyond the disapproving register, lucre in older English could mean simply gain or profit in a neutral sense, but the KJV uses the word predominantly in the disapproving phrase, and the modern reader does well to hear it that way. Filthy lucre names not money itself (which is morally neutral as a means of exchange) but the love of money and the willingness to dishonor God or harm one’s neighbor for the sake of it. The love of money, Paul says, is the root of all evil (1 Tim 6:10); the love of filthy lucre is the same root showing itself specifically in the ministry, the office, the teaching that has been bought by it. The recovery of the doctrine is the recovery of a serious qualification for the office: men whose ministry is plainly not motivated by money, whose pattern of life shows them content with what they have, whose teaching is not for sale to the highest bidder—these are the men the New Testament calls to feed the flock of God, and the church saturated with such men is the church the apostles intended.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines LUCRE as gain in money or goods; profit; usually in an ill sense, or with the sense of something base or unworthy; in scripture, the disapproving phrase filthy lucre names dishonest or motivating-of-the-wrong-kind gain, especially in church office.
webster_full: LUCRE, n. — Gain in money or goods; profit; usually in an ill sense, or with the sense of something base or unworthy. Not greedy of filthy lucre (1 Tim 3:3).
LUCRATIVE, a. — Profitable; gainful; producing profit or gain; as a lucrative trade.
scriptures: 1 Timothy 3:3
Not given to wine, no striker, not greedy of filthy lucre; but patient, not a brawler, not covetous.
Titus 1:7
For a bishop must be blameless, as the steward of God; not selfwilled, not soon angry, not given to wine, no striker, not given to filthy lucre.
Titus 1:11
Whose mouths must be stopped, who subvert whole houses, teaching things which they ought not, for filthy lucre’s sake.
1 Peter 5:2
Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind.
corruption_summary: The doctrine of filthy lucre is corrupted by the prosperity-gospel and platform-evangelical traditions that have explicitly tied ministry to financial advancement and made teaching for money respectable—and by the inverse asceticism that treats money itself as evil, against Scripture’s distinction between money (neutral) and the love of money (the root of all evil).
corruption_paragraphs: The prosperity-gospel and certain platform-evangelical traditions have explicitly tied ministry to financial advancement, made the size of the offering a measure of the minister’s anointing, sold spiritual goods at premium prices, and produced a class of teachers whose pattern of life manifestly contradicts the apostolic qualification of not greedy of filthy lucre. The corruption is structural and pastoral: when ministry-as-profession is shaped by the same incentive structures as ministry-as-commerce, the apostolic Paul who refused even legitimate apostolic support (1 Cor 9:14-18) so that he might not be a burden looks like a strange figure, and Tit 1:11’s diagnosis (teaching things which they ought not, for filthy lucre’s sake) becomes uncomfortably contemporary. The recovery is the recovery of the qualification as a real test: men whose pattern of life shows them genuinely uninfluenced by money in their ministerial choices, whose teaching is not for sale, whose comforts are modest, whose financial dealings can be examined without scandal—these are the men the New Testament calls to the office.

The opposite corruption is the inverse asceticism that treats money itself as evil, refuses any compensation for ministerial work, and reads the New Testament’s warnings against filthy lucre as condemnations of money as such. Scripture refuses this. Paul explicitly affirms that the workman is worthy of his hire (1 Tim 5:18) and that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel (1 Cor 9:14); congregations are commanded to support their pastors and missionaries; the apostolic teaching distinguishes the use of money (legitimate) from the love of money (forbidden). The biblical balance is precise. Money is morally neutral; ministerial compensation is legitimate; filthy lucre is the love of gain that motivates ministerial choices, willing-to-teach-error-for-money, willing-to-sell-spiritual-goods-at-a-profit, willing-to-shape-message-for-financial-gain. Recover both ends. Refuse the prosperity-platform corruption that has made ministry-for-money respectable, and refuse the ascetic corruption that treats money itself as evil. The biblical pattern is content, honest, non-money-motivated ministers receiving appropriate support from their churches and free from the love of gain that the New Testament names as the structural disqualification for office.
roots_summary: Latin lucrum (gain, profit); KJV’s filthy lucre renders Greek aischrokerdēs (shamefully-greedy)—the love of gain that disqualifies for church office and characterizes the false teachers whose mouths must be stopped.
roots_lines: Greek aischrokerdēs (G146) — greedy of base gain (1 Tim 3:3, 8; Tit 1:7).
Greek aischrokerdōs (G147) — for the sake of base gain (1 Pet 5:2).
Greek kerdos (G2771) — gain, profit (used both negatively and, in Phil 1:21, positively: “to die is gain”).
Latin lucrum — gain, profit (the etymology of lucre).
usage: Not greedy of filthy lucre—the apostolic qualification structural to the office of elder and deacon.
Teaching things which they ought not, for filthy lucre’s sake—Tit 1:11 names the false-teacher pattern whose motivation is money.

Prosperity-platform Christianity has made ministry-for-money respectable; ascetic over-correction treats money itself as evil; biblical doctrine distinguishes money (neutral) from the love of money (root of all evil).

etymology: Old French par aventure, “by chance, perhaps,” from Latin per (through, by) + adventura (a happening, a coming-to-pass). Renders the Hebrew ’ūlay, “perhaps,” and the Greek tachá and mēpote in conditional and contingent contexts.
biblical_def: Peradventure is the KJV’s elegant archaic adverb for perhaps, by chance, if it may be—naming the contingent or uncertain. The word carries an antique register and frequently appears in moments of high pastoral or covenantal seriousness. Abraham’s great intercession for Sodom uses it across the negotiation: peradventure there be fifty righteous within the city... peradventure there shall lack five of the fifty righteous... peradventure there shall be forty found there... peradventure thirty... peradventure twenty... peradventure ten (Gen 18:24-32)—the patriarch leaning into the LORD’s mercy with the cautious uncertainty proper to a creature pleading with the Judge of all the earth. The patriarchs’ peradventures recur across Genesis: peradventure he will accept of me says Jacob of the brother he is approaching after the long years away (Gen 32:20). Solomon’s wise counsel in Proverbs uses it: contend not with a man without cause, if he have done thee no harm... lest thou learn his ways, and get a snare to thy soul—and similar prudential peradventures in the wisdom literature. The verb’s pastoral usefulness across the Bible is several. It is the proper register for the creature’s speech before the Sovereign God in matters where the outcome is hidden in His counsels (Abraham’s intercession). It is the proper register for the patriarch’s anticipation of the brother’s response in matters of relational reconciliation (Jacob’s approach to Esau). It is the proper register for the wise counsel that admits the contingencies of life’s providences (Solomon’s warnings). And it is the proper register for the apostolic and pastoral counsel that acknowledges what is hoped but cannot be presumed (Paul’s peradventure in 2 Tim 2:25, of God granting repentance to those that oppose). The KJV’s retention of peradventure over the more colorless perhaps carries the register of one who is speaking with weight, with care, with the dignity proper to matters in which God’s sovereignty and the creature’s contingency meet.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines PERADVENTURE as perhaps; it may be; by chance; in scripture, the elegant archaic adverb for what is hoped but cannot be presumed.
webster_full: PERADVENTURE, adv. — By chance; perhaps; it may be. Peradventure there be fifty righteous within the city (Gen 18:24).
PERADVENTURE, n. — Chance; doubt; as, the conclusion is admitted without any peradventure.
scriptures: Genesis 18:24
Peradventure there be fifty righteous within the city: wilt thou also destroy and not spare the place for the fifty righteous that are therein?
Genesis 32:20

And say ye moreover, Behold, thy servant Jacob is behind us. For he said, I will appease him with the present that goeth before me, and afterward I will see his face; peradventure he will accept of me.
2 Timothy 2:25
In meekness instructing those that oppose themselves; if God peradventure will give them repentance to the acknowledging of the truth.
Romans 5:7
For scarcely for a righteous man will one die: yet peradventure for a good man some would even dare to die.
corruption_summary: Peradventure is corrupted (by the standards of modern accessibility) by being replaced with the colorless perhaps—losing the register of weighty conditional speech that suits Abraham’s intercession, Jacob’s approach to Esau, Paul’s instruction to those that oppose, and the wisdom literature’s prudential counsel.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern translations uniformly replace peradventure with perhaps or it may be. The substitution is grammatically defensible; the loss is rhetorical. Peradventure carries a register of weight, dignity, and the acknowledgment of contingency that perhaps in modern usage has not retained. Abraham’s intercession for Sodom, with its six-fold peradventure, is a sustained piece of cautious pleading before the Judge of all the earth—the verb in the patriarch’s mouth is doing rhetorical work in setting the tone of his negotiation with the LORD. Replace each peradventure with perhaps, and the rhetorical weight thins; replace each with maybe, and the patriarch begins to sound like a man chatting about weekend plans. The KJV’s antique register is here doing pastoral and rhetorical work the modernizations cannot replicate.

The recovery of the KJV vocabulary is therefore not antiquarianism. It is the recovery of a register of speech the modernizations have lost, in a Bible that uniquely shaped the English Christian piety of four centuries. Modern translations have their proper uses (the new convert, the reader unable to parse the older idiom, the comparative cross-check); but the saint who learns to read the KJV in its own register hears Scripture in a vocabulary register the modernization has, sometimes, quietly flattened. Peradventure is a small specimen of the larger pattern: a word that does work the colorless substitute cannot do, retained in the KJV, available to the saint who will learn its register. The case for retaining it is the same case for retaining the King James Bible itself: not the rejection of modernization but the recognition that the older language is, in many of its places, doing things the modernizations cannot reproduce.
roots_summary: Old French par aventure (by chance) from Latin per + adventura; renders Hebrew ’ūlay (perhaps) and Greek tachá, mēpote in conditional contexts—the elegant archaic adverb for what is hoped but cannot be presumed.
roots_lines: Hebrew ’ūlay (H194) — perhaps, peradventure (Gen 18:24-32; Josh 14:12; 1 Sam 14:6; 1 Kgs 18:5; Jonah 1:6).
Greek tachá (G5029) — perhaps, peradventure (Rom 5:7; Phlm 15).
Greek mēpote (G3379) — lest perhaps, if perhaps (2 Tim 2:25).
Old French par aventure — by chance (the etymological source).
usage: Peradventure there be fifty righteous within the city—Abraham’s six-fold intercession for Sodom is sustained by the verb’s cautious-pleading register.
Peradventure is the proper register for matters where the outcome is hidden in God’s sovereign counsels and the creature speaks with weight and care.
Modern perhaps flattens the rhetorical work the KJV’s peradventure performs; the older word carries weight the substitute has lost.

etymology: Old English weaxan, “to grow, increase.” Distinct from the noun wax (the substance). The KJV preserves the archaic verb in many places where modern translations use grew or became.
biblical_def: Wax as a verb in the KJV means to grow, increase, become—an Old English word that has all but disappeared from modern English usage except in a few residual phrases (wax and wane, wax eloquent). The KJV preserves it across many passages, both of literal growth and of moral or spiritual increase. Of the boy John the Baptist: and the child grew, and waxed strong in spirit (Luke 1:80). Of the child Jesus: and the child grew, and waxed strong in spirit, filled with wisdom: and the grace of God was upon him (Luke 2:40). Of the apostles after the first persecution: they spake the word of God with boldness... and the word of God increased; and the number of the disciples multiplied... and many of the priests were obedient to the faith (Acts 4:31, 6:7—the underlying verb is the same). Of the gospel’s spread under persecution: but the word of God grew and multiplied (Acts 12:24). The verb is therefore positive in many of its biblical uses. But it has a negative register also. The love of many shall wax cold, Christ says of the latter-day apostasy (Matt 24:12)—the verb naming the inverse increase, the growing-cold of love that should have been growing warm. Wax old as doth a garment, Hebrews 1:11 says of the heavens and earth which shall pass away—the increase that is the aging toward dissolution. Wax worse and worse, Paul says of evil men and seducers in the last days (2 Tim 3:13). The KJV’s retention of the verb has therefore a structural usefulness: it captures the picture of growing, increasing, becoming-more, in a single Old English word that can be applied to physical maturation, spiritual growth, moral increase (in either direction), and cosmic dissolution. Modern translations have to choose between grew, became, increased, got, depending on context; the KJV says waxed, and the reader who knows the verb knows what it covers.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines WAX as to increase in size; to grow; to become larger; to pass from one state to another; in scripture, to grow physically, spiritually, or morally in either direction.
webster_full: WAX, v.i. — 1. To increase in size; to grow; to become larger; as the waxing and waning of the moon. 2. To pass from one state to another; to become; as, the days wax cold. The love of many shall wax cold (Matt 24:12).
WAXING, ppr. — Increasing in size or extent; growing; becoming.
scriptures: Luke 1:80
And the child grew, and waxed strong in spirit, and was in the deserts till the day of his shewing unto Israel.
Luke 2:40
And the child grew, and waxed strong in spirit, filled with wisdom: and the grace of God was upon him.
Matthew 24:12
And because iniquity shall abound, the love of many shall wax cold.
Hebrews 1:11-12

They shall perish; but thou remainest; and they all shall wax old as doth a garment; And as a vesture shalt thou fold them up, and they shall be changed: but thou art the same, and thy years shall not fail.
corruption_summary: Wax as a verb has been functionally lost in modern English, replaced with several scattered alternatives (grew, became, increased); the loss is a small specimen of the general thinning of English vocabulary, and the KJV reader who recovers the verb recovers also a register of growth-and-becoming that the substitutes cannot quite reproduce.
corruption_paragraphs: Wax as a verb has been functionally lost from modern English usage, surviving only in a few residual phrases (wax eloquent, wax and wane) that retain the word as a stylized fossil rather than as a living verb. Modern translations therefore have no single equivalent and must scatter the KJV’s consistent wax across several different words (grew, became, increased, got) depending on context. The trade has its accessibility gains and its rhetorical losses. The KJV’s consistent verb captures the underlying picture of growing-becoming, applicable to the boy John, the boy Jesus, the spreading gospel, the cooling love, the aging heavens, and the worsening of evil men, in a single Anglo-Saxon word that the modernizations cannot quite consolidate. The reader who has learned the KJV verb can hold all these uses together in his mind under one word; the reader of the modernizations cannot.

This is, as with holpen and peradventure, a small specimen of the general thinning of English vocabulary that the modernization of the Bible has both registered and accelerated. The older English had more words for shades of meaning the modern English has flattened. Wax meant something the substitutes do not quite capture: not just grow, not just become, not just increase, but the specific Anglo-Saxon verb for growing-becoming that runs from the cradle through the cooling and on to the dissolution of the heavens. Recover the word in the KJV, and one recovers also access to a register modern English has narrowed. The case is not for the rejection of modern translations but for the recognition that the older vocabulary is doing work the substitutes cannot always perform, and the saint who knows both is the better-served reader of both.
roots_summary: Old English weaxan (to grow, increase); used in the KJV to render several Greek and Hebrew growth-verbs: auxanō (to grow), palaioō (to grow old), psuchō (to grow cold)—a single Anglo-Saxon word covering the picture of growing-becoming.
roots_lines: Old English weaxan — to grow, increase (the etymological root).
Greek auxanō (G837) — to grow, increase (Luke 1:80; 2:40; Acts 6:7; 12:24; 19:20).
Greek palaioō (G3822) — to make old, declare old (Heb 1:11; 8:13).
Greek psuchō (G5594) — to grow cool, cold (Matt 24:12).
usage: The child grew, and waxed strong in spirit—the same verb for John (Luke 1:80) and Jesus (Luke 2:40), capturing physical-and-spiritual maturation in a single word.
The love of many shall wax cold—the negative use: the growing-becoming that runs in the direction of dissolution.
Modern translations scatter wax across grew, became, increased; the KJV’s single Anglo-Saxon verb captures the underlying picture the substitutes thin out.

pos: v. (archaic past tense of wit, to know)
etymology: Archaic past tense of the Old English verb witan, “to know.” The verb wit (to know) survives in modern English only in the phrase to wit (that is to say) and the noun wit (cleverness); the past tense wist is preserved chiefly in the KJV.
biblical_def: Wist is the archaic past tense of the Old English verb witan, “to know,” preserved in the KJV in a handful of memorable places where the disciples or other figures knew not some matter. The verb is the same root as German wissen (to know) and the modern English noun wit (sense, cleverness)—the underlying meaning is to have perception, to understand, to know. The KJV’s most-quoted use is in the boyhood narrative of Christ: at twelve years old, lingering in the temple while His parents had departed, He is found by Mary and Joseph after three days’ search; and to their reproach (Son, why hast thou thus dealt with us? behold, thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing) He replies: how is it that ye sought me? wist ye not that I must be about my Father’s business? (Luke 2:49). The verb in the boy Jesus’s mouth is the gentle did you not know?—a question that introduces the deepest theological claim of the Lucan boyhood narrative: His Father is not Joseph but God. The KJV’s other notable uses include the disciples on the Mount of Transfiguration: when Peter offered to make three tabernacles, Mark notes parenthetically he wist not what to say; for they were sore afraid (Mark 9:6)—a candid disclosure that Peter’s impulsive proposal came out of confusion rather than insight. Peter on the night of his release from prison: and Peter went out, and followed him; and wist not that it was true which was done by the angel; but thought he saw a vision (Acts 12:9). Joshua in his rebuke to the children of Israel: thou hast spoiled us... that we wist not. Samson, after the locks of his strength had been shaved: and he wist not that the LORD was departed from him (Judg 16:20)—one of the most pathos-laden uses in Scripture. The verb’s biblical pattern therefore captures the moments of human not-knowing under God’s providence: the disciples not knowing what to say, Peter not knowing the deliverance was real, Samson not knowing the Spirit had departed, the boy Jesus gently noting His parents’ not knowing what He must be about. Wist not is therefore the KJV’s register for those moments of human ignorance that God’s narrator records with the dignity of the older verb—moments where the saint, faced with the same providence, would do well to ask whether he too is wisting what he should be about or has missed what the LORD is doing.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines WIST as the archaic past tense of wit (to know); knew; in scripture, used in the KJV for moments of human not-knowing under God’s providence.
webster_full: WIST, v. — Archaic past tense of wit (to know); knew. Wist ye not that I must be about my Father’s business? (Luke 2:49). He wist not what to say (Mark 9:6).
WIT, v.t. or n. — (Archaic verb) To know; to be informed. Now used chiefly in the phrase to wit, that is to say.
scriptures: Luke 2:49
And he said unto them, How is it that ye sought me? wist ye not that I must be about my Father’s business?
Mark 9:6
For he wist not what to say; for they were sore afraid.
Acts 12:9
And he went out, and followed him; and wist not that it was true which was done by the angel; but thought he saw a vision.
Judges 16:20

And she said, The Philistines be upon thee, Samson. And he awoke out of his sleep, and said, I will go out as at other times before, and shake myself. And he wist not that the LORD was departed from him.
corruption_summary: Wist is corrupted (by the standards of modern accessibility) by retaining a verb that has dropped out of modern English usage; the loss in the modern translations is small in vocabulary but large in cadence, especially in the boyhood narrative of Christ and in the pathos-laden disclosure of Samson’s not knowing the LORD had departed from him.
corruption_paragraphs: Wist has dropped out of modern English usage, and modern translations uniformly replace it with knew. The substitution is grammatically defensible; the rhetorical effect is different. Wist ye not that I must be about my Father’s business? carries a gentle archaic dignity in the boy Jesus’s mouth that didn’t you know I had to be in my Father’s house? simply does not replicate. The cadence of the older verb suits the cadence of the boyhood narrative; the modern verb thins the register. He wist not what to say of Peter on the Mount carries the candor of an older idiom; he didn’t know what to say reads like contemporary narrative. The most pathos-laden use of all—and he wist not that the LORD was departed from him of Samson—is one of Scripture’s most devastating one-liners, and the older verb carries the gravity the moment requires.

This is, again, the general case for the KJV’s antique vocabulary as a bearer of register modern English has lost. The argument is not that modernization is wrong but that it has costs the modernizers do not always reckon. Wist is a verb that adds dignity, antique cadence, and a slight psychological-distance from the contemporary register that often serves the biblical narrative well—especially in the boyhood narrative where the divine Son speaks to His earthly parents with both filial gentleness and theological weight, and in the Samson narrative where the most devastating disclosure of the chapter is rendered in the most measured voice. Modern translations have their proper uses; the KJV with its wists and wists-not has its proper uses too; and the saint who reads both reads Scripture in two registers, neither of which is the only legitimate one. The case for the older register is not for the rejection of the newer but for the preservation of what the newer cannot always carry.
roots_summary: Old English witan (to know), past tense wist; same root as German wissen and modern English wit; preserved in the KJV in moments of human not-knowing under God’s providence (Samson, Peter, the disciples, the boy Jesus to His parents).
roots_lines: Old English witan — to know; the verb of wist and wist not.
Greek oida (G1492) — to know (the chief verb behind wist in NT uses).
Hebrew yāda (H3045) — to know (the OT cousin verb; Judg 16:20 of Samson).
German wissen — to know (the cognate from the same root).
usage: Wist ye not that I must be about my Father’s business?—the boy Jesus’s gentle question carrying the deepest theological claim of the Lucan boyhood narrative.
And he wist not that the LORD was departed from him—Samson at Judg 16:20, one of Scripture’s most devastating disclosures.
Modern knew is grammatically equivalent but rhetorically thinner; wist carries antique dignity and psychological distance that often serve the biblical narrative well.

pos: adj. or n. (past participle of obsolete won, “to be accustomed”)
etymology: From Old English gewunod, past participle of gewunian (to be accustomed, dwell). The verb won in this sense is obsolete; wont survives as an adjective (he was wont to do thus) and a noun (as his wont was).
biblical_def: Wont is the KJV’s archaic word for what is customarily or habitually done—a person’s settled practice, his usual pattern, the thing he was accustomed to do. The word survives in modern English chiefly in the phrase as is his wont; the KJV uses it across both testaments to render the Hebrew and Greek words for customary practice. Of the LORD Himself, of Christ, of the apostles, of various figures across Scripture, the verb captures the pattern: this was the manner from the beginning, as the manner of the priests was; and Jesus went, as he was wont, to the mount of Olives (Luke 22:39); and he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up: and, as his custom was, he went into the synagogue on the sabbath day, and stood up for to read (Luke 4:16—custom there is the cousin word). The narrative function of wont is several. It captures the settled patterns of life that are the visible texture of any person’s discipleship—Christ’s wont of going to the Mount of Olives, His wont of synagogue attendance on the Sabbath, His wont of withdrawing to pray, His wont of teaching. It captures the institutional patterns by which the priestly orders or civic offices operated. It captures the personal patterns by which figures like Daniel were known—Daniel as he was wont opening his windows toward Jerusalem and praying three times a day, even when the decree forbade it. The narrative significance of wont is therefore important: it makes visible the long patterns of a life lived in a particular way, the disciplines that constitute the texture of discipleship, the personal and institutional habits that the LORD and His people maintain across the years. Where Scripture says of Christ as he was wont, it names a pattern that had become so settled in His earthly life that His disciples could predict where He would be in the evening, what He would do on the Sabbath, how He would withdraw to pray. The disciple’s life is to be similarly patterned: settled wonts of prayer, of Word, of gathering, of worship, of generosity, of confession, of family devotion—patterns the people who know him can name as what he is wont to do, and that constitute the long arc of faithful discipleship across his years.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines WONT as accustomed; used; as in the phrase he was wont to do this; in scripture, used of Christ’s settled patterns of life (Mount of Olives, synagogue, prayer) and of the personal patterns of the saints.
webster_full: WONT, a. or n. — Accustomed; used; as, he was wont to do this. And Jesus went, as he was wont, to the mount of Olives (Luke 22:39).
WONT, v.i. — To be accustomed or habituated; to be used. (Now chiefly archaic; survives in the adjective and the phrase.)
scriptures: Luke 22:39
And he came out, and went, as he was wont, to the mount of Olives; and his disciples also followed him.
Mark 10:1
And he arose from thence, and cometh into the coasts of Judaea by the farther side of Jordan: and the people resort unto him again; and, as he was wont, he taught them again.
Daniel 6:10

Now when Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house; and his windows being open in his chamber toward Jerusalem, he kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did aforetime.
Luke 4:16
And he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up: and, as his custom was, he went into the synagogue on the sabbath day, and stood up for to read.
corruption_summary: Wont is corrupted (by the standards of modern accessibility) by its near-disappearance from modern English; the loss of the word coincides with the loss in the contemporary church of the rich category of settled patterns of life that the biblical wonts of Christ and the saints make visible.
corruption_paragraphs: Wont has nearly disappeared from modern English usage, surviving chiefly as a stylized phrase in literary writing. Modern translations replace it with custom, usually, habit, or rephrase the construction entirely. The vocabulary loss is small; the loss of the underlying category, however, is large. Wont names a settled pattern of life, the visible texture of disciplines maintained across years. Jesus went, as he was wont, to the mount of Olives tells us not merely where He went that evening but what His pattern was—the long-settled habit of withdrawing to the Mount, predictable enough that His disciples followed without instruction and Judas knew where to find Him. The biblical narrative is rich with such wonts: Daniel’s windows-toward-Jerusalem prayer thrice daily; Christ’s synagogue attendance on every Sabbath; Paul’s reasoning in the synagogues on the Sabbath days; the patterns of life that constituted the visible discipleship of each.

The loss of the category in contemporary Christianity is a real pastoral concern. The believer often lives without settled wonts: prayer is fit in when convenient, Scripture-reading is sporadic, gathering is according to inclination, fasting is rare or non-existent, family worship is occasional rather than disciplined. The visible texture of discipleship—the patterns that the people who know him can name as what he is wont to do—has thinned to almost nothing. The recovery is the recovery of the disciplines themselves, settled over time into the patterns of life that Scripture describes of Christ and the saints. The KJV’s wont is therefore not merely a vocabulary item but a window into a discipleship category the contemporary church needs: the settled, predictable, long-pattern life that Christ Himself modeled and that the saints have always exhibited as the texture of mature faith. Recover the disciplines that make the word applicable, and the disciple recovers what it is to be wont to do the things that mark a life formed by Christ.
roots_summary: Old English gewunod (accustomed), past participle of obsolete won (to be accustomed); preserved in the KJV in passages naming the settled patterns of life of Christ, Daniel, and the saints—the visible texture of discipleship.
roots_lines: Old English gewunian — to be accustomed, dwell; root of wont.
Greek ethō (G1486) — to be accustomed; used in Luke 4:16 (“as his custom was”).
Greek ethos (G1485) — custom, habit (Acts 17:2, Paul’s synagogue reasoning “as his manner was”).
Hebrew qūm + adverbial construction — conveying the habitual practice (often in narrative contexts of Daniel-type patterns).
usage: Jesus went, as he was wont, to the mount of Olives—Christ’s settled pattern of evening withdrawal to the Mount, predictable enough that Judas knew where to find Him.
Daniel’s windows-toward-Jerusalem prayer thrice daily and Christ’s Sabbath synagogue attendance are exemplars of biblical wonts: settled patterns of life as the visible texture of discipleship.
Loss of the word and loss of the category coincide; recovery of disciplined patterns is recovery of what it means to be wont to do the things that mark a life formed by Christ.

etymology: Old English fægen, “glad, joyful, eager.” In KJV usage chiefly adverbial: gladly, willingly, eagerly. The word survives only in stylized literary usage in modern English.
biblical_def: Fain in the KJV means gladly, willingly, eagerly—an Old English adverb expressing the disposition of the soul that would gladly do or have a thing, often paired with an unfulfilled wish or unattained desire. The word’s most famous biblical use is the prodigal son: and he would fain have filled his belly with the husks that the swine did eat: and no man gave unto him (Luke 15:16). The young man, having wasted his substance with riotous living and now reduced to feeding swine in a far country, would gladly have eaten the very husks the pigs ate—the deepest indignity in his desperate hunger—and no man gave unto him. The verb would fain carries the picture of yearning desire that cannot be satisfied: the disposition is there, the will is there, the hunger is acute, but the satisfaction is withheld. Other notable KJV uses include Acts 26:28: then Agrippa said unto Paul, Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian. And Paul’s response (v. 29): I would to God, that not only thou, but also all that hear me this day, were both almost, and altogether such as I am, except these bonds. Acts 28:27, Paul’s quotation of Isaiah 6 in interpretation of Israel’s hardening: lest they should see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and should be converted, and I should heal them. Job 27:22: for God shall cast upon him, and not spare: he would fain flee out of his hand. The verb’s pastoral usefulness is its capture of the soul’s registered desire—particularly in the contexts of unsatisfied longing (the prodigal’s hunger), of ardent wish for another’s good (Paul’s wish for Agrippa), of the unbeliever’s vain flight from God’s judgment (Job 27), and of the soul’s reach after what is desired but unattained. Fain is the older English’s precise way of saying gladly-but-not-attained, willingly-but-not-realized, eagerly-but-withheld; and the prodigal’s would-fain-have-eaten-the-husks remains one of the most poignant single phrases in Scripture, naming the depth of his fall in the dignity of the older idiom.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines FAIN as gladly; with joy or pleasure; with preference; usually with would, as in he would fain go; in scripture, the older English adverb capturing the disposition of glad-but-unattained desire (most famously the prodigal’s would-fain-have-eaten-the-husks).
webster_full: FAIN, adv. — Gladly; with joy or pleasure; with preference. Usually employed with the auxiliary would; as, he would fain go.
FAIN, a. — Glad; pleased; rejoiced. (Archaic adjectival use.)
scriptures: Luke 15:16
And he would fain have filled his belly with the husks that the swine did eat: and no man gave unto him.

Then Agrippa said unto Paul, Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian. And Paul said, I would to God, that not only thou, but also all that hear me this day, were both almost, and altogether such as I am, except these bonds.
For God shall cast upon him, and not spare: he would fain flee out of his hand.
Luke 13:31
The same day there came certain of the Pharisees, saying unto him, Get thee out, and depart hence: for Herod will fain kill thee.
corruption_summary: Fain is corrupted (by the standards of modern accessibility) by being functionally lost from modern English; the loss in modern translations is small in vocabulary but real in cadence, especially in the prodigal’s would-fain-have-eaten-the-husks, where the older idiom carries the depth of his fall in a register the modern equivalents flatten.
corruption_paragraphs: Fain has dropped from modern English usage almost entirely. Modern translations of Luke 15:16 read he longed to fill his belly with the pods that the pigs were eating or he would have eagerly filled his belly with the carob pods; the rhetorical effect is different. Would fain have filled his belly with the husks carries an antique register of dignified pathos that the modernizations have not retained. The prodigal’s fall is portrayed with the gravity the older idiom supplies: a young man, who had wasted his father’s substance with riotous living, now reduced to a longing that would have been content with what the pigs ate, and even that was not granted. The reader who knows would fain hears the verse in its full pathos; the reader who hears only the modern equivalents hears a flatter version of the same incident.

This is, as with the other KJV archaisms covered in this batch, a small specimen of the larger pattern. The older vocabulary carries registers of pathos, dignity, and cadence the modern English equivalents have, in many places, lost. The case for the older language is not the rejection of the newer but the recognition that the KJV is doing work the modernizations sometimes cannot replicate—and the saint who reads the KJV in its own idiom recovers access to a register of Scripture that has shaped English Christian piety for four centuries and that is not entirely available in the modernizations. Would fain is one of the smaller and more poignant of these registers, and the prodigal’s use of it remains one of the most affecting single phrases in the English Bible.
roots_summary: Old English fægen (glad, eager); used in the KJV chiefly with would to express glad-but-unattained desire, most famously in the prodigal’s would-fain-have-eaten-the-husks (Luke 15:16).
roots_lines: Old English fægen — glad, eager (the etymological root).
Greek epithumeō (G1937) — to desire, long for (Luke 15:16, behind would fain).
Greek thelō (G2309) — to will, desire (Luke 13:31, behind will fain).
Hebrew chāphets (H2654) — to delight in, desire (the OT cousin verb of glad desire).
usage: He would fain have filled his belly with the husks that the swine did eat: and no man gave unto him—the prodigal’s fall named in the dignity of the older idiom.
Would fain captures glad-but-unattained desire: the disposition is there, the satisfaction is withheld; the older adverb names what modern English equivalents flatten.
Modern translations replace fain with longed, eagerly, or rephrase the construction; the older word carries antique cadence and pathos the substitutes have lost.

etymology: From Old French sucurre, from Latin succurrere, “to run beneath, run to help,” from sub- (under) + currere (to run). The picture is literal: to run beneath or alongside as help. Renders the Greek boētheō, “to help,” and antilambanō, “to take hold of, support.”
biblical_def: Succor in the KJV is the antique English verb for to help, aid, run to one’s assistance—a word whose Latin etymology (sub- + currere, to run beneath) captures the picture of literal coming-alongside-with-help. The verb’s most theologically weighty NT use is in the high-priestly application to Christ in Hebrews 2:18: for in that he himself hath suffered being tempted, he is able to succour them that are tempted. The Greek boētheō means to run to help upon a cry; Christ’s qualification to succor the tempted is precisely that He Himself was tempted, suffered being tempted, and now stands ready to come to the aid of His people in their parallel trials. The verb has its OT-narrative uses also. The Syro-Phoenician woman’s cry to Christ for her daughter: Lord, help me—in the KJV often rendered with the succoring picture (Matt 15:25). Paul’s commendation of Phebe to the Romans: that ye receive her in the Lord, as becometh saints, and that ye assist her in whatsoever business she hath need of you: for she hath been a succourer of many, and of myself also (Rom 16:1-2). The biblical doctrine of succor therefore has two principal applications. Christologically, Christ Himself succors the tempted—He hears the cry of His people under trial, runs to their assistance, and brings the help they need precisely because He has been tempted Himself and knows the weight. Ecclesiologically, the saints succor one another—Phebe’s succor of many and of Paul himself is a Pauline model, and the church saturated with such mutual succor is the church living out the body-of-Christ identity in concrete embodied care. The recovery of the word is therefore the recovery of two doctrines: the high-priestly succor of Christ to His tempted people, and the mutual succor of saints to one another in the body. Both belong together. Christ succors the tempted; His saints, taught of Him, succor one another in turn.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SUCCOR as to run to, or run to support; hence, to help or relieve when in difficulty, want or distress; to assist and deliver from suffering; in scripture, the verb of Christ’s high-priestly aid to the tempted and of the saints’ mutual aid in the body.
webster_full: SUCCOR, v.t. — To run to, or run to support; hence, to help or relieve when in difficulty, want or distress; to assist and deliver from suffering. He is able to succour them that are tempted (Heb 2:18).
SUCCOR, n. — Aid; help; assistance; particularly assistance that relieves and delivers from difficulty, want or distress. For she hath been a succourer of many (Rom 16:2).
scriptures: Hebrews 2:18
For in that he himself hath suffered being tempted, he is able to succour them that are tempted.
2 Corinthians 6:2
...behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation.
Romans 16:1-2

I commend unto you Phebe our sister, which is a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea: That ye receive her in the Lord, as becometh saints, and that ye assist her in whatsoever business she hath need of you: for she hath been a succourer of many, and of myself also.
Matthew 15:25
Then came she and worshipped him, saying, Lord, help me.
corruption_summary: Succor is corrupted (by the standards of modern accessibility) by retaining a word that has nearly dropped from modern usage; the loss in modern translations is the loss of the picture-in-the-etymology of running-beneath-with-help that suits both Christ’s high-priestly aid to the tempted and the saints’ mutual aid in the body.
corruption_paragraphs: Succor has nearly dropped from modern English usage, surviving chiefly in literary and military contexts. Modern translations replace it with help, aid, or rephrase the construction. The substitution is grammatically defensible; the loss is in the picture the etymology supplies. Succor—literally to run beneath, run to assist—captures the action of help in motion, the picture of running to one’s side when the cry goes up, the urgency of help applied to the moment of need. Help in modern usage is more static and abstract; succor still carries the picture of the runner arriving with what is needed. The KJV’s retention of the word preserves both the picture and the register.

The doctrine the word supports is also worth recovering. Christ’s high-priestly succor (Heb 2:18) is one of the most pastorally tender doctrines of the New Testament: the One who runs to the aid of His tempted people is qualified to do so precisely because He has been tempted Himself, has suffered being tempted, and brings to the help He renders the deep sympathy of one who knows the weight. The believer in temptation is therefore not merely sympathized with by a distant deity but actively succored by an experienced high priest who runs to His side. And the church’s mutual succor (Phebe, Rom 16:2) is patterned on Christ’s own: saints running to the aid of fellow-saints in need, the body-of-Christ ministry rendered concrete in the practical care of brothers and sisters in their actual distresses. Recover the word, recover the doctrine, and recover the practice: Christ’s succor to the tempted, and the saints’ succor to one another, are both meant to fill the contemporary church as they filled the apostolic one.
roots_summary: Latin succurrere (to run beneath, run to help) from sub- + currere; renders Greek boētheō (to help upon a cry) and antilambanō (to take hold of, support)—the picture of running-to-help, applied to Christ’s high-priestly aid to the tempted and the saints’ mutual aid in the body.
roots_lines: Latin succurrere — to run beneath, run to help (the etymological root).
Greek boētheō (G997) — to help upon a cry (Heb 2:18; Matt 15:25; Mark 9:22, 24; Acts 16:9; 21:28; 2 Cor 6:2; Rev 12:16).
Greek antilēmptōr (G484) — one who takes hold of, helper, succorer.
Greek prostatis (G4368) — a female protector, helper, succorer (Rom 16:2 of Phebe).
usage: He is able to succour them that are tempted—Christ’s high-priestly qualification to run to the aid of His tempted people, grounded in His own temptation and suffering.
Phebe, a succourer of many, and of myself also—Pauline model of the saint’s mutual succor in the body of Christ.
Succor captures the picture of running-with-help that help in modern usage has flattened; the older verb names both Christ’s high-priestly aid and the saints’ embodied mutual care.

etymology: Old English twægen, the masculine form of two; survived in modern English only in a few stylized phrases (never the twain shall meet) and in the KJV.
biblical_def: Twain is the KJV’s archaic word for two, particularly in contexts of pairs that constitute a unity or that come together in unique theological union. The most theologically weighty use is in Christ’s teaching on marriage, citing Genesis 2: have ye not read, that he which made them at the beginning made them male and female, And said, For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be one flesh? Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder (Matt 19:4-6). Christ’s use of twain at the marriage-doctrine’s heart is structurally significant. The marriage of one man and one woman creates a new unity such that they are no more twain, but one flesh: the two have become one in a covenantal union grounded in creation itself and not to be undone by human action. The Greek duo behind twain here is the ordinary number-word, but the older English word carries a slight archaic dignity that suits the gravity of the marriage-doctrine. Paul applies the same Genesis 2 text to the deeper mystery of Christ and the church in Ephesians 5:31: for this cause shall a man leave his father and mother, and shall be joined unto his wife, and they two shall be one flesh. Other notable KJV uses of twain include the veil of the temple rent in twain from the top to the bottom at the moment of Christ’s death (Matt 27:51), and several proverbial uses (let thine arrows be twain in 2 Kgs 9:24, etc.). The verb’s most enduring application is the marriage-and-union picture: the twain becoming one flesh, no longer twain but one—a creation-grounded unity that human action does not have authority to dissolve. The recovery of the older word is small; the recovery of the underlying doctrine is large: the marriage of one man and one woman creates a one-flesh union that human dissolution does not have authority over, and the saint receives the marriage-covenant as a creation-ordinance with the gravity Christ Himself assigned to it.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines TWAIN as two; in scripture, used by Christ in His marriage-teaching (they twain shall be one flesh, Matt 19:5) and at the rending of the temple veil at the crucifixion (Matt 27:51).
webster_full: TWAIN, n. — Two. They twain shall be one flesh (Matt 19:5). The veil of the temple was rent in twain (Matt 27:51).
TWO, n. — One and one; the second cardinal number; a couple; a pair.
scriptures: Matthew 19:5-6

And said, For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be one flesh? Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.
Matthew 27:51
And, behold, the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom; and the earth did quake, and the rocks rent.
Genesis 2:24
Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.
Ephesians 5:31-32
For this cause shall a man leave his father and mother, and shall be joined unto his wife, and they two shall be one flesh. This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church.
corruption_summary: Twain is corrupted (by the standards of modern accessibility) by its near-disappearance from modern English; more pressingly, the doctrine the word supports—the creation-grounded one-flesh union of one man and one woman in marriage—is corrupted by the present age’s redefinition of marriage and the wholesale denial of the creation-ordinance Christ’s use of twain rests upon.
corruption_paragraphs: Twain has dropped from modern English usage almost entirely. The vocabulary loss is small; but the doctrine the word supports—Christ’s teaching on marriage as the one-flesh union of one man and one woman—has come under sustained cultural assault in the present age. Where Christ said they twain shall be one flesh, wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh; what therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder, the present age claims authority to redefine the categories Christ Himself names: twain in marriage need not be one man and one woman; the joining is not God-grounded but socially constructed; the dissolution is at the parties’ discretion; the one-flesh union has no creation-grounding to preserve. The recovery is the recovery of Christ’s appeal to Genesis 2 as the controlling text on marriage: God made them male and female; for this cause a man cleaves to his wife; they twain are one flesh; God has joined; let no man put asunder. Each clause stands; the structure stands; and the redefinitions and dissolutions of the present age fall against the wall of Christ’s own teaching.

Beyond the marriage-doctrine, twain’s other great biblical use is at the moment of Christ’s death: the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom. The twain there is the literal two pieces into which the temple veil split; but the theological significance is that the access between the holy place and the holiest of all, kept closed throughout the Old Testament administration, has been opened by Christ’s atoning death. The torn veil is the architectural confession of the gospel: the way into the holiest is now made manifest, and the saints have boldness to enter by the blood of Jesus (Heb 10:19-22). Rent in twain from the top to the bottom—the older word again carries antique gravity to the moment; the modern torn in two conveys the fact but flattens the register. The KJV vocabulary, retained where it is doing rhetorical work, is part of the dignity with which the English Bible has, for four centuries, set forth the great doctrines of the faith.
roots_summary: Old English twægen (two, masculine form); renders Greek duo (two)—a number-word whose older English form carries antique dignity, especially in Christ’s marriage-teaching (they twain shall be one flesh) and at the rending of the temple veil at the crucifixion.
roots_lines: Old English twægen — two (masculine form; the etymological root).
Greek duo (G1417) — two (the cardinal number).
Hebrew sh’nayim (H8147) — two (the OT cardinal).
Greek dichotomē (G1371) — cutting in two (the related verb behind cut asunder).
usage: They twain shall be one flesh; wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh—Christ’s marriage-teaching grounds the union in creation and forbids human dissolution.
The veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom—the architectural confession at Christ’s death that the way into the holiest is now open.
Modern two conveys the number; the older twain carries antique dignity that suits the gravity of marriage-doctrine and the moment of the veil’s rending.
